faqs.question: How much house can I afford?
faqs.answer: Housing costs should not exceed 28% of gross income. Total debt should stay under 36%.

faqs.question: What's included in a mortgage payment?
faqs.answer: Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance (PITI). Plus PMI if down payment is under 20%.

faqs.question: How do extra payments help?
faqs.answer: Extra payments reduce principal faster, cutting total interest and loan term.

faqs.question: What credit score do I need?
faqs.answer: Conventional: 620+. FHA: 580+ (3.5% down). VA: typically 620+.

faqs.question: Should I get pre-approved?
faqs.answer: Yes, pre-approval shows sellers you're serious and helps set your budget.

faqs.question: How is monthly payment calculated?
faqs.answer: Using the loan amount, interest rate, and term in the standard amortization formula.

faqs.question: What's the difference between APR and interest rate?
faqs.answer: APR includes fees and reflects true cost. Interest rate is just the rate charged on principal.

faqs.question: Should I choose a longer or shorter term?
faqs.answer: Shorter terms have higher payments but less total interest. Longer terms are more affordable monthly.

faqs.question: How do I calculate total interest paid?
faqs.answer: Total Interest = (Monthly Payment × Number of Payments) - Principal

faqs.question: Can I pay off my loan early?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, but check for prepayment penalties. Extra payments save significant interest.

faqs.question: What's a good interest rate for a car loan?
faqs.answer: New cars: 4-7%. Used cars: 5-10%. Excellent credit gets the lowest rates.

faqs.question: How much should I put down on a car?
faqs.answer: Ideally 20% for new cars, 10% for used. More down payment = less interest paid.

faqs.question: Should I choose a longer loan term?
faqs.answer: Longer terms have lower payments but cost more in interest. Try to keep it under 60 months.

faqs.question: How does trade-in affect my loan?
faqs.answer: Trade-in reduces the amount financed, lowering your payment and total interest.

faqs.question: Is 0% financing really free?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, but you might get a better deal with cash rebate + regular financing.

finance/interest.introText: Whether you're earning interest on savings or paying interest on a loan, our calculator shows exactly how interest accumulates over time.
finance/interest.formula: Simple: I = P×r×t | Compound: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)

benefits.title: Final Amount
benefits.description: See total value at end of term

faqs.question: What's the difference between simple and compound interest?
faqs.answer: Simple interest is calculated only on principal. Compound interest is calculated on principal plus accumulated interest.

faqs.question: How does compounding frequency affect earnings?
faqs.answer: More frequent compounding = more interest. Daily compounding earns more than monthly.

faqs.question: What is APY vs APR?
faqs.answer: APY includes compounding effect, showing true annual return. APR doesn't account for compounding.

faqs.question: How do I calculate interest for any period?
faqs.answer: For partial periods, use the daily rate (annual ÷ 365) times number of days.

faqs.question: Why does compound interest matter?
faqs.answer: Over long periods, compound interest grows exponentially, making huge differences.

finance/compound.name: Compound Interest

finance/compound.heroSubtitle: See the power of compound growth
finance/compound.introText: Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Our calculator shows exactly how powerful compounding can be for your savings.

benefits.title: Visual Growth Chart
benefits.description: Watch your wealth compound over time

faqs.question: What is compound interest?
faqs.answer: Interest calculated on initial principal AND accumulated interest. Your money earns money on its earnings.

faqs.question: How often should interest compound?
faqs.answer: More frequent is better. Daily compounding earns more than monthly or annual.

faqs.question: What's the Rule of 72?
faqs.answer: Divide 72 by interest rate to estimate years to double. At 8%, money doubles in ~9 years.

faqs.question: How much difference does compound interest make?
faqs.answer: $10,000 at 7% for 30 years: Simple = $31,000. Compound = $76,123.

faqs.question: When should I start investing?
faqs.answer: As early as possible. Time is the most powerful factor in compound growth.

benefits.description: Divide equally among any number of people

benefits.title: Total Breakdown
benefits.description: See tip, total, and per-person amounts

faqs.question: How much should I tip at a restaurant?
faqs.answer: Standard is 15-20% of pre-tax bill. 20%+ for excellent service.

faqs.question: Do I tip on tax?
faqs.answer: Technically tip on pre-tax amount, but tipping on total is common and generous.

faqs.question: What about tipping for takeout?
faqs.answer: 10-15% is appreciated for takeout, especially for large orders.

faqs.question: How do I calculate 20% quickly?
faqs.answer: Move decimal one place left (10%), then double it. $50 bill = $5 × 2 = $10 tip.

faqs.question: Should I tip on alcohol?
faqs.answer: Yes, include full food and beverage total when calculating tip.

finance/salary.name: Salary
finance/salary.metaTitle: Salary Calculator - Convert Hourly to Annual & Net Pay | CalcMaster

finance/salary.heroSubtitle: Calculate your annual salary and take-home pay
finance/salary.introText: Convert between hourly, weekly, monthly, and annual salary. Our calculator also estimates your take-home pay after federal and state taxes.
finance/salary.formula: Annual = Hourly × Hours/Week × 52 | Take-Home = Gross - Taxes - Deductions

faqs.question: How do I convert hourly to annual salary?
faqs.answer: Multiply hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks. $20/hr × 40 × 52 = $41,600/year.

faqs.question: What is take-home pay?
faqs.answer: Gross salary minus all deductions: federal tax, state tax, Social Security, Medicare, benefits.

faqs.question: How much of my salary goes to taxes?
faqs.answer: Typically 20-35% depending on income and location. Our calculator estimates this.

faqs.question: How do I calculate my effective tax rate?
faqs.answer: Total taxes paid ÷ gross income × 100. This is usually lower than your marginal bracket.

faqs.question: Should I negotiate salary or hourly?
faqs.answer: Salary provides stability, hourly may pay more with overtime. Consider your work patterns.

faqs.question: What are the 2026 tax brackets?
faqs.answer: 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37% for federal. Brackets adjust annually for inflation.

faqs.question: What's the difference between marginal and effective tax rate?
faqs.answer: Marginal is your highest bracket. Effective is total tax ÷ total income (always lower).

faqs.question: Should I take standard or itemized deduction?
faqs.answer: Take whichever is higher. In 2026, standard is $14,600 single, $29,200 married.

faqs.question: How do tax credits work?
faqs.answer: Credits reduce tax directly, dollar for dollar. More valuable than deductions.

faqs.question: When are taxes due?
faqs.answer: April 15th for most. Extensions give until October 15th to file (not pay).

finance/inflation.name: Inflation
finance/inflation.metaTitle: Inflation Calculator - See Purchasing Power Over Time | CalcMaster
finance/inflation.metaDescription: Free inflation calculator shows how money's value changes over time. Calculate purchasing power, inflation-adjusted amounts, and historical price changes.
finance/inflation.heroSubtitle: See how purchasing power changes over time
finance/inflation.introText: What was $100 worth in 1990? What will $100 be worth in 2030? Our inflation calculator shows how the value of money changes over time.
finance/inflation.formula: Future Value = Present Value × (1 + Inflation Rate)^Years

faqs.question: What is inflation?
faqs.answer: The rate at which prices increase over time, reducing purchasing power of money.

faqs.question: What's the average inflation rate?
faqs.answer: Historically about 3% per year in the US, though it varies significantly year to year.

faqs.question: How does inflation affect savings?
faqs.answer: If your savings earn less than inflation, you're losing purchasing power.

faqs.question: What is CPI?
faqs.answer: Consumer Price Index - measures average change in prices paid by consumers over time.

faqs.question: Why do I need to account for inflation?
faqs.answer: For retirement planning, investments, and understanding true salary growth.

finance/budget.introText: Take control of your finances with our budget calculator. We use the proven 50/30/20 rule to help you allocate income to needs, wants, and savings.

benefits.title: Surplus Check
benefits.description: Are you living within your means?

faqs.question: What is the 50/30/20 rule?
faqs.answer: 50% of income to needs (housing, food), 30% to wants (entertainment), 20% to savings/debt.

faqs.question: What counts as needs vs wants?
faqs.answer: Needs: housing, utilities, food, insurance, minimum debt payments. Wants: everything else.

faqs.question: How do I stick to a budget?
faqs.answer: Track spending, automate savings, review monthly, and adjust as needed.

faqs.question: What if I can't do 50/30/20?
faqs.answer: Adjust ratios to your situation. 60/20/20 or 70/20/10 are okay while building income.

faqs.question: How much emergency fund do I need?
faqs.answer: 3-6 months of expenses. Start with $1,000 then build from there.

finance/retirement.name: Retirement
finance/retirement.metaTitle: Retirement Calculator - How Much Do You Need? | CalcMaster
finance/retirement.metaDescription: Free retirement calculator shows if you're on track. Calculate how much you need to retire, when you can retire, and how long savings will last.
finance/retirement.introText: Will you have enough to retire? Our calculator projects your retirement savings, shows if you're on track, and helps you plan for the future you want.

benefits.title: Projection Chart
benefits.description: See your wealth grow to retirement

faqs.question: How much do I need to retire?
faqs.answer: Rule of thumb: 25× your annual expenses. $50K/year expenses = $1.25M needed.

faqs.question: What is the 4% rule?
faqs.answer: Withdraw 4% of savings in year 1, then adjust for inflation. Historically lasts 30 years.

faqs.question: When can I retire?
faqs.answer: When investments can cover expenses. Earlier requires more savings or lower expenses.

faqs.question: Should I include Social Security?
faqs.answer: Yes, but don't rely on it fully. It replaces about 40% of pre-retirement income.

faqs.question: What's a good retirement savings rate?
faqs.answer: 15-20% of income including employer match. More if starting late.

longTailVariants.title: How Much to Retire

finance/401k.introText: Your 401k is one of the best retirement tools. Our calculator shows how contributions, employer match, and compound growth build your nest egg.
finance/401k.formula: Future Value = Contributions × (1 + r)^n + Employer Match × (1 + r)^n

benefits.title: Employer Match
benefits.description: Don't leave free money on the table

faqs.question: How much should I contribute to my 401k?
faqs.answer: At minimum, enough to get full employer match. Ideally 15-20% of salary total.

faqs.question: What is employer matching?
faqs.answer: Free money! Common match is 50% of first 6% you contribute = 3% extra salary.

faqs.question: What's the 401k limit?
faqs.answer: 2026: $23,000 under 50, $30,500 if 50+. Limits increase annually.

faqs.question: Traditional vs Roth 401k?
faqs.answer: Traditional = tax deduction now, taxed at withdrawal. Roth = no deduction, tax-free withdrawal.

faqs.question: When can I withdraw from 401k?
faqs.answer: 59½ without penalty. Early withdrawal has 10% penalty plus taxes (with some exceptions).

finance/roi.name: ROI
finance/roi.metaTitle: ROI Calculator - Calculate Return on Investment | CalcMaster
finance/roi.metaDescription: Free ROI calculator shows your return on investment. Calculate percentage return, annualized ROI, and compare different investment options.
finance/roi.introText: ROI (Return on Investment) measures how much money you made relative to what you invested. Essential for comparing investment opportunities.
finance/roi.formula: ROI = (Gain from Investment - Cost of Investment) / Cost × 100%

benefits.title: Percentage Return
benefits.description: See ROI as a clear percentage

faqs.question: What is ROI?
faqs.answer: Return on Investment - the percentage gain or loss relative to the amount invested.

faqs.question: What is a good ROI?
faqs.answer: Depends on investment type. Stock market average is ~10%/year. Real estate often 8-12%.

faqs.question: How do I calculate annualized ROI?
faqs.answer: Annualized ROI = ((1 + ROI)^(1/years) - 1) × 100. Allows fair comparison across time periods.

faqs.question: Does ROI include dividends?
faqs.answer: Yes, total return includes capital gains plus any income like dividends or rent.

faqs.question: What's the difference between ROI and profit?
faqs.answer: Profit is the dollar amount. ROI is the percentage, which lets you compare different sized investments.

finance/amortization.heroSubtitle: See your complete loan payment schedule
finance/amortization.introText: Amortization is how loan payments are split between principal and interest over time. Our calculator shows you exactly where every payment goes.
finance/amortization.formula: Interest = Balance × Monthly Rate | Principal = Payment - Interest

benefits.title: Full Schedule
benefits.description: Every payment for the life of the loan

faqs.question: What is amortization?
faqs.answer: The process of paying off a loan through regular payments that cover both principal and interest.

faqs.question: Why does so much go to interest early on?
faqs.answer: Interest is calculated on remaining balance. Higher balance = more interest. As you pay down, more goes to principal.

faqs.question: How do extra payments help?
faqs.answer: Extra payments go directly to principal, reducing interest charged and shortening the loan term.

faqs.question: What's negative amortization?
faqs.answer: When payments don't cover interest, so balance grows. Avoid loans with this feature.

faqs.question: Can I get an amortization schedule from my lender?
faqs.answer: Yes, lenders must provide this. Our calculator helps you understand it and plan extra payments.

finance/debt-payoff.metaDescription: Free debt payoff calculator compares snowball vs avalanche methods. See how long to become debt-free and how much interest you'll save.
finance/debt-payoff.introText: Multiple debts? Our calculator compares the debt snowball and avalanche methods to help you find the fastest, cheapest path to becoming debt-free.
finance/debt-payoff.formula: Snowball: Smallest balance first | Avalanche: Highest interest first

benefits.title: Snowball Method
benefits.description: Pay smallest debts first for quick wins

benefits.title: Avalanche Method
benefits.description: Pay highest interest first to save money

benefits.title: Debt-Free Date
benefits.description: See when you'll be free of debt

faqs.question: What is the debt snowball method?
faqs.answer: Pay minimums on all debts, throw extra at the smallest balance. Quick wins build momentum.

faqs.question: What is the debt avalanche method?
faqs.answer: Pay minimums on all debts, throw extra at highest interest rate. Saves the most money.

faqs.question: Which method is better?
faqs.answer: Avalanche saves more money. Snowball has psychological wins. Choose what you'll stick with.

faqs.question: How much extra should I pay toward debt?
faqs.answer: As much as possible while maintaining emergency fund. Even $50 extra makes a difference.

faqs.question: Should I save or pay off debt first?
faqs.answer: Build $1,000 emergency fund first, then attack debt aggressively.
